summary: This wiki-style note on Armenia covers several themes: the Armenian Genocide and the resulting diaspora, ancient and medieval Armenian kingdoms, the Adana massacre, the short-lived First Republic, Soviet-era rule, and the modern republic's education, economy, military and international ties. It mixes historical summaries with statistics from the late Soviet period and early 1990s.
one_line: Overview of Armenia's history from ancient kingdoms and the Armenian Genocide through Soviet rule to independence, with notes on education, the military and the economy.
key_facts: The Armenian Genocide caused widespread emigration that led to the settlement of Armenians in various countries of the world.
In 1989 some 58% of Armenians over age fifteen had completed their secondary education, and 14% had a higher education.
In 1992 Yerevan State University had eighteen departments, about 1,300 teachers and about 10,000 students.
Arnold J. Toynbee's research estimated that 600,000 Armenians died during deportation from 1915–16, but this figure covers only the first year of the Genocide.
The International Association of Genocide Scholars places the death toll of the Armenian Genocide at "more than a million".
The total number of people killed in the Armenian Genocide has been most widely estimated at between 1 and 1.5 million.
Turkish authorities deny the Armenian Genocide took place to this day.
In April 1909 the Adana massacre in the Adana Vilayet of the Ottoman Empire resulted in the deaths of as many as 20,000–30,000 Armenians.
The Orontid Dynasty established the first geographical entity called Armenia by neighboring populations in the late 6th century BC, within the Achaemenid Empire.
King Artaxias I made Armenia fully sovereign from the Seleucid Empire in 190 BC, beginning the rule of the Artaxiad dynasty.
Armenia reached its height between 95 and 66 BC under Tigranes the Great, becoming the most powerful kingdom of its time east of the Roman Republic.
The First Republic of Armenia declared its independence on 28 May 1918 under the leadership of Aram Manukian, after the Transcaucasian Democratic Federative Republic dissolved.
The TSFSR existed from 1922 to 1936, when it was divided into the Armenian SSR, Azerbaijan SSR and Georgian SSR.
The modern Republic of Armenia became independent in 1991 during the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
Armenia is a member of the Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO) and participates in NATO's Partnership for Peace (PiP) program.
